newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan's Bhutto says her father's blood betrayed.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan's Bhutto says her father's blood betrayed.

text.p: Pakistan's deposed prime minister Benazir Bhutto poured scorn on President Farooq Leghari on Monday, accusing the man who ousted her of executing a coup and betraying the blood of her hanged father.
"I feel not only personally betrayed," Bhutto told Reuters Television in an interview. "I believe he (Leghari) betrayed the blood of my father."
Benazir's father, Zulfikar Ali Bhutto, was Pakistan's first popularly elected prime minister, ruling from 1971 to 1977 when he was toppled by army chief General Mohammad Zia-ul-Haq.
Zulfikar was hanged in April 1979 on a disputed conviction for conspiring to commit a political murder.
Benazir said Leghari, who sacked her three-year-old government with a pre-dawn order last Tuesday, had vowed not to use his constitutional power to dissolve the National Assembly.

"It was his pledge to us, if elected he would never resort to a device which has been foisted upon the constitution by the junta," she said, speaking at her sprawling official residence perched above the capital Islamabad. She moves out on Tuesday.
"My father gave his blood for this country and for parliamentary democracy. Our workers were hanged for parliamentary democracy," she said.
"I feel he (Leghari) let down the blood, blood that had been shed for this cause. I feel very emotional about this because he knows he was with us. He knows the sacrifices."
Leghari, who once served in Benazir's cabinet, was hand-picked by his mentor in 1993. But Pakistan's political crisis has laid bare a high-stakes struggle between the two.

Benazir said: "Power changed him and I could see how he was changing with power, becoming more arrogant. He is not used to it. He was always number two. But I thought that he's a decent man and that that spark of decency is in his heart."
Leghari's order dismissing Bhutto's government cited corruption, mismanagement and extra-judicial killings among other accusations which he said had virtually paralysed the government.
But describing her dismissal and the imposition of a caretaker government, Bhutto said it was "the presidential, civilian equivalent of martial law".

Bhutto, wearing a bright purple silk "shalwar kameez" and beige scarf around her head, was relaxed and brimming with confidence that a legal challenge she plans to mount this week will return her to power soon.
"The Supreme Court should restore the assembly within a month," she said.
She said that late on Sunday she visited her husband, who has been detained without charges near Islamabad for nearly a week. His morale was high, and they laughed together, she said.

But Bhutto, who clawed her way back to power in 1993 after being sacked a first time in 1990, had nothing but sharp words for Leghari and the caretaker government, saying they were trying to "eliminate" her politically with a smear campaign and would fabricate charges.

"I know the president and his coterie went around world capitals, foreign offices, international press, and made all sorts of horrendous charges against my husband, my cabinet colleagues and myself," she said.
"What we are witnessing today is a trampling of human rights and trampling of democratic norms."
She reiterated a call for Leghari, whom she called biased, to step down and yield power to a neutral, interim government.
Bhutto said she planned to go to Karachi on Saturday and then on to Lahore "to begin contact with the people".
Asked why few of her supporters came into the streets last week after her dismissal, she said her Pakistan People's Party had not issued a protest call.
Would she now issue the call? "We want to wait for the (Supreme) Court decision, and then we want to examine the situation," she said.
